blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
User Interface (UI) plays a crucial role in today’s desktop software, mobile applications, and online websites. It serves as
a visual bridge between a software application and end-users through which they can interact with each other [30, 33].
Good UI designs are essential to the success of a software application and can gain loyalty from the software users [19].
However, designing a good UI can be challenging, even for experienced designers. On the one hand, designers need to
strive for creative ideas and follow many design rules and principles, such as fluent interactivity, universal usabili

summary.text: Argues that wireframing is a common way to express UI design intent, and that mid-fidelity wireframes add real content and semantic icons to low-fidelity sketches at a higher cost in time and effort, which no previous work has streamlined. Introduces WireGen, which fine-tunes LLMs on Rico UI screens and view hierarchies to generate mid-fidelity wireframes from design-intent descriptions, then post-processes them with semantic icons, text typography and UI guidelines. Reports 77.5% significantly better generations than two in-context learning baselines, 84.5% against three ablation models, and a user study with five professional designers.

blocks.title: Designing with Natural Language
blocks.content:
2.1
Mobile UI Wireframe
Wireframing plays a pivotal role in many types of creative activities because of its highly visual nature and its flexibility
for creation and manipulation: designers can create and imagine any kind of visual content, and continuously revise
it without being constrained by unnecessary details [36, 49, 79]. Subsequently, mobile UI wireframing is well-suited

summary.text: Opens subsection 2.1, "Mobile UI Wireframe": wireframing suits creative work because it is highly visual and can be created, manipulated and revised without unnecessary detail. The text breaks off mid-sentence.

blocks.title: Abstract
blocks.content:

prototypes by wireframing. With the essential of UI wireframe as a profession in the UI design process, many academic
research [44, 57] and commercial graphic tools including Adobe PhotoShop [2], Sketch [10], and Figma [6] are developed
to allow designers to sketch the UI wireframes at multiple detail levels from low-fidelity to mid-fidelity and final UI
(as shown in Fig. 2). Low-fidelity wireframes serve as the design’s starting point that tends to be fairly rough, created
w

summary.text: Despite its heading, this block continues the related-work discussion of UI wireframing: tools from SILK to Photoshop, Sketch and Figma support low- to mid-fidelity wireframes, and human-AI co-creation systems such as Swire help designers find inspiration or generate layouts. The authors note that these still require designers to sketch a low-fidelity wireframe and add content, whereas their work generates mid-fidelity wireframes directly from a design-intent description; the block ends by opening subsection 2.2 on bridging natural language and UI screens.

Some research specifically generates semantically alt-text labels for UI elements [16, 17, 20, 27, 31, 32, 32, 34, 78]. These
studies attempt to learn the latent representation of UIs to generate natural language understanding. On the contrary,

The interest in involving natural language as a f

summary.text: Reviews work linking natural language and UIs (screen summarisation, alt-text generation) and text-to-image generation, noting that DALLE, Stable Diffusion and MidJourney misspell text and lack design coherence and that a prior UI Generator yields only low-fidelity layouts. Subsection 2.3 describes zero-shot, few-shot and fine-tuned prompting of LLMs and motivates fine-tuning for UI wireframing. Section 3 then outlines WireGen's three phases: data preparation, model fine-tuning and output beautification.

blocks.title: Prepare Dataset of UI Wireframes and Descriptions
blocks.content:
3.1.1
Mid-fidelity Wireframes and Descriptions. While there are many low-fidelity wireframe datasets available [15,
25, 51, 68, 69], none of the prior work studies on mid-fidelity wireframes. This is because mid-fidelity wireframes go
beyond the shape, placeholders, and “lorem ipsum” text of low-fidelity wireframes to include real content, semantic
icons, interactive elements, etc. However, manual labeling of wireframes can be prohibitively expensive. To that end,
5
Feng et al.
we propose a novel approach to automatically collect a set of representations of mid-fidelity wireframes. As shown in

summary.text: Builds a training set by treating Rico's 66k Android UI screens (9.7k apps, 27 categories) as mid-fidelity wireframes and pairing them with Screen2Words descriptions written by 85 professional labelers. Screens are converted to HTML plus a style sheet by a depth-first traversal of the view hierarchy, mapping native classes to HTML tags (Table 1) from the resource_id, class, text, content_desc and bounds properties, with absolute positioning for layout.

blocks.title: Fine-tune Large Language Models with Best Practice
blocks.content:
Since the LLMs are not specifically designed to understand the UI design patterns, we fine-tune the LLMs with the natural
language description as the input and the UI wireframe in HTML syntax as the output (the same learning objective as
the pre-trained model). The implementation of fine-tuning process is not a trivial task [50], which can significantly
influence the performance of LLMs. To that end, we summarize three highly sensitive aspects in fine-tuning LLMs,
denoting training data selection, model selection, and hyperparameter configuration, and detail our implementation
informed by the

summary.text: Fine-tunes with descriptions as input and HTML wireframes as output, and details three sensitive choices: 1,000 training samples selected by app (191 apps, 27 categories) to avoid leakage; the GPT model Turbo (gpt-3.5-turbo), chosen as the most advanced and strong at understanding code; and hyperparameters of learning rate 0.1, batch size 256, 4 epochs, temperature 0.65, a 4,096-token maximum length and </html> as the stop sequence.

blocks.content: Figure 5 — Before/after comparison of a fitness app wireframe: the left "Raw Generation" screen has text-only buttons (return, settings, more options), overlapping "Healthy"/"Get Started" text, a duplicated "see more" button and an off-screen text block, marked with blue letters A-F; the centre lists "Semantic Icons", "Text Typography" and "UI Guidelines" with small icons; the right "Post Processing" screen shows a back arrow, gear and three-dot icons, resized text and corrected layout.

blocks.title: Transform Raw Generation into Beautiful UI Wireframe
blocks.content:
After fine-tuning process, we prompt the LLMs with a simple description of design intent to generate a HTML syntax of
mid-fidelity wireframes. However, programming languages like HTML and CSS are not easy for designers to understand.
We wish to hide the programming hardships under-the-hood to reduce the designer’s burden. Besides, the LLMs may
not fully capture the intricacies of the design knowledge behind the UI designs. To this goal, we propose post-processing
methods to transform the raw HTML syntax generation into intuitive, fluent, and interactive UI wireframes. An example
of the post-pr

summary.text: Post-processes the raw HTML into usable wireframes in three ways: semantic icons, chosen by prompting the LLM against a top-10 icon-semantics category derived by open coding 4,000 Rico icons; text typography, framed as an optimisation over wrapping and font size that minimises wasted block space; and heuristics for three UI-guideline flaws found in 100 generations, namely occlusion, duplication and out-of-bound elements.

blocks.title: Evaluation
blocks.content:
In this section, we conduct experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of our fine-tuned LLMs in generating mid-
fidelity UI wireframes.
4.1

summary.text: Introduces Section 4, which runs experiments on how effectively the fine-tuned LLMs generate mid-fidelity UI wireframes.

blocks.title: Research Questions
blocks.content:
RQ1: (Performance of Fine-tuning) Does the optimization of fine-tuning correlate with better UI wireframe
generations? For RQ1, we evaluate the effectiveness of fine-tuning the LLMs, compared with widely-used in-context
learning baseline approaches (e.g., zero-shot and few-shot).
RQ2: (Performance of Variations) Do the variations of the LLMs result in better UI wireframes? For RQ2, we
present the comparison among the variations of GPT models (e.g., Curie, Babbage, Ada) to demonstrate the performance
of using Turbo as the model.
4.2

summary.text: Poses two research questions: RQ1, whether fine-tuning yields better wireframes than zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning; and RQ2, whether Turbo outperforms the other GPT variants Curie, Babbage and Ada.

blocks.title: Testing Data
blocks.content:
We collect the data as discussed in Section 3.1 as our experimental dataset. Since we leverage 1,000 sample data to
fine-tune the LLMs, we first remove these data to avoid potential bias. To evaluate the LLMs’ generalizability and
diversity, we randomly select 2 apps from each category. In total, we collect 100 UI textual descriptions as the input
prompts to generate UI wireframes. Note that we do not use the corresponding UI screens as the ground-truth because
the generative LLMs may create reasonable UI wireframes but deviate from the ground-truth.
11
Feng et al.
Fig. 6. Examples of promptin

summary.text: The test set is 100 UI textual descriptions, two apps per category, drawn from the Section 3.1 data after removing the 1,000 training samples. The original UI screens are not used as ground truth, because a generated wireframe may be reasonable yet differ from them.

blocks.title: Annotation Methodology
blocks.content:
We recruit two people who had backgrounds in UI/UX design and art practice to rate the UI wireframe designs generated
by our LLMs. At the beginning of the experiment, we first give them an introduction to our study and ask them to
read UI/UX design books for 30 minutes to deepen the design principles. Given the natural language descriptions and
a grid of UI wireframe designs, annotators are then asked to independently rate which designs in the grid are either
significantly better generations or significantly worse generations. Note that we randomly shuffle the designs in the
grid, so that the

summary.text: Two people with UI/UX design and art backgrounds, after 30 minutes reading design books, independently rated shuffled grids of generated wireframes as significantly better or significantly worse without knowing which model produced each; they were paid $20 per hour.

blocks.title: RQ1: Performance of Fine-tuning
blocks.content:
4.4.1
Baselines. To demonstrate the advantage of fine-tuning to master the domain-specific task of UI wireframe
generation, we compare it with two widely-used in-context learning methods as baselines, including zero-shot learning
and few-shot learning. Note that all the experiment settings (e.g., model, hyperparameter, etc.) are the same.
Zero-shot learning: It predicts the results without any training samples. The general idea behind zero-shot learning
is the LLMs train on a wide collection of different databases and workloads and can thus generalize to a completely
new task and workload with

summary.text: Compares WireGen with zero-shot and few-shot prompting (K of 1 to 2 examples) under identical settings. WireGen's generations were rated significantly better 85.5% of the time on average, while zero-shot and few-shot received 51.5% and 44.5% significantly worse ratings, with a Cohen's kappa of 0.32; zero-shot produced relevant elements without regard to layout, and few-shot improved layouts but generalised poorly.

blocks.content: Figure 7 — Grid of grey mobile wireframes comparing models "Ada", "Babbage", "Curie" and "WireGen" (columns) on two prompts (rows): "general settings page" (ranging from a sparse Add Location screen, a plain Settings list, and a Settings/More Apps tabbed screen with checkboxes, to WireGen's General Settings with Backup/Restore, Appearance, Notify Me, Send Feedback and About Us items with descriptions) and "welcome page" (from a title with an image placeholder to WireGen's Welcome screen with image, Twitter/Facebook buttons and Sign In/Sign Up buttons).

blocks.title: RQ2: Performance of Variations
blocks.content:
4.5.1
Baselines. As our implementation of LLMs GPT offers different models to support different levels of tasks, we set
up the other models, including Curie, Babbage, and Ada, as the baselines to compare with our model. To guarantee
the fairness of the experiment, we fine-tune these models on the training dataset using the same training settings as
discussed in Section 3.2.
4.5.2

summary.text: Sets up Curie, Babbage and Ada as the RQ2 baselines, each fine-tuned on the same training data with the same settings as Turbo.

blocks.title: Results
blocks.content:
baseline models, e.g., 76.5% vs 11.5%, 10.5%, 1.5% for Curie, Babbage, and Ada, respectively. Both Curie and Babbage
show the tendency to generate average UI wireframes (78% and 82.5%), while Ada underperforms with 81.5% of UI
wireframes rated to be significantly worse. We report the inter-rater reliability score of 0.28 in Cohen’s kappa, which
represents a fair agreement, which we think is valid considering the highly subjective nature of the task (picking “better”
or “worse” UI wireframe designs).
Fig. 7 shows some examples generated by our model (Turbo) and the baselines (Curie, Babbage, an

summary.text: Turbo was rated significantly better in 76.5% of cases, against 11.5%, 10.5% and 1.5% for Curie, Babbage and Ada; Curie and Babbage mostly produced average wireframes and 81.5% of Ada's were rated significantly worse, with a Cohen's kappa of 0.28. Examples show Turbo generating more detailed elements, such as subtitles under titles, which the authors attribute to it being the most powerful model.

blocks.title: User Study
blocks.content:
In language, there are many ways to say the same thing in different words. We conduct a user study to gain insights
into the usefulness of our model in assisting designers with UI wireframe generation with real-world descriptions.
5.1

summary.text: Introduces a user study of how useful the model is in helping designers generate UI wireframes from real-world descriptions, since the same thing can be said in many different words.

blocks.title: Participants
blocks.content:
We invite five UI/UX designers to participate in our experiments by word-of-mouth and through online advertisements
on social media and design communities.
• P1: Visual designer, 6 years of working experience, now working at a large multinational company, responsible
for international app design and design innovation.
• P2: Interaction designer/product designer from a medium-sized company, with 4 years of working experience.
Her work mainly focuses on smart devices.
• P3: Designer from a large IT company for 2 years with a focus on mobile advertising user experience design.
• P4: Visual design

summary.text: Five UI/UX designers took part, recruited by word of mouth and online advertisements, with 2 to 6 years of experience in visual, interaction and product design at companies of various sizes and at a design-sharing community.

blocks.title: Procedure
blocks.content:
The user studies were conducted online via the Zoom platform. Each participant took about one hour to complete. Each
study session began with a short interview in which the participants were asked about their professional background

summary.text: In one-hour Zoom sessions, participants generated a login-page wireframe by editing a given prompt, then used WireGen freely on their own scenarios alongside other tools, and rated it on a 5-point scale: effective for inspiration (4.4), relevant to the prompts (4.0) and diverse (3.6). All judged it better than wireframe-sharing, layout-generation and text-to-image tools, and they asked for integration with design software as a plugin and for representative images in place of alt-text.

blocks.title: Discussion
blocks.content:
In Section 4 and Section 5, we evaluate and examine WireGen ’s effectiveness and usefulness for automatically generating
mid-fidelity UI wireframes from natural language descriptions. We see several opportunities to improve the performance
of our LLMs. For example, we see that training on a large dataset can deliver better results. However, due to budget
constraints, we only use 1,000 data for training. Once we have enough budget, we can improve the performance of the
LLMs by incorporating more data.
The LLMs are obviously not omnipotent, and still, fail to provide ready-to-use outputs in many

summary.text: Names limitations and future work: training on only 1,000 samples for budget reasons, post-processing based on a small-scale study of design flaws, and prompts built only from screens and view hierarchies. Proposes multimodal prompts, iterative design through chat, and retrieving similar existing UI designs by encoding generated wireframes with Screen2Vec.

blocks.title: Conclusion
blocks.content:
This paper introduces WireGen, a new method for exploring human-AI collaboration in mid-fidelity UI wireframe
creation. Inspired by the success of generative Large Language Models in creating innovative ideas, we purpose to
inherit LLMs’ in-context ability from billions of web resources to create mid-fidelity UI wireframes. Since LLMs are
not designed for UI understanding and creation, we fine-tune it with thousands of UI data, including screens and view
hierarchies, to help the LLMs master UI design knowledge. With the fine-tuned LLMs, we prompt a simple description
of design intent to genera

summary.text: Restates that WireGen fine-tunes LLMs on thousands of UI screens and view hierarchies, generates raw wireframes from design-intent descriptions and post-processes them, and that experiments and a user study show it outperforms baselines and ablated models and is useful in practice.
